details.analysis:
TL;DR: Over the past five years AMD’s revenues moved from ~$20B (2020) to a volatile path peaking in the mid‑$40–60B range before a partial 2025 value in the SQL extract, while NVIDIA clearly accelerated faster on the chart; AMD’s revenue trajectory implies targeted investments to capture data‑center and AI share rather than broad capex across fabs [1]. The line_multi chart shows AMD’s lumpy, cyclical revenue pattern versus NVIDIA’s steeper breakout, which helps explain AMD’s capex and investment focus on product/packaging and ecosystem partnerships.

Key points:
- Revenue context (SQL): AMD annual revenues in the extract — $20.0B (2020), $38.78B (2021), $47.49B (2022), $39.19B (2023), $60.69B (2024), $15.12B (2025 partial) — indicating large year‑to‑year swings that typically drive targeted, project‑level capex [1].  
- Chart takeaway: AMD’s flatter, more variable line vs NVIDIA’s sharp rise implies AMD funds selective growth initiatives (data center CPUs/accelerators, packaging, IP/R&D) rather than massive, sustained fab spending.  
- Capex drivers for AMD (why it spends): direct R&D for next‑gen Zen CPUs and CDNA GPUs; advanced packaging (chiplet and 3D stacking investments, co‑development with foundries); integration of Xilinx FPGA tech and associated toolchain/platform work; customer‑driven server validation and system engineering (data center deployments require design wins and integration spend).  
- Capital structure & partner model: as a fabless company AMD’s capital expenditures skew toward test/assembly tooling, design platforms, and co‑investment commitments with foundries (TSMC) rather than owning wafer fabs — this reduces headline capex but raises strategic spend on partnerships and long‑lead engineering. [1]

Watchouts: The SQL annuals capture revenue but not capex line items; reconcile with AMD’s CAPEX and R&D line items in cash flow and footnotes to quantify actual spend — also check fiscal definitions and partial‑year rows before modeling future capex needs.
